MutableKey k = new MutableKey("A");              // equals and hashCode both use id
Map<MutableKey, String> m = new HashMap<>();
m.put(k, "value");
k.id = "B";                                      // mutate a field used in hashCode
System.out.println("get after mutation: " + m.get(k) + " | size: " + m.size()
        + " | containsValue: " + m.containsValue("value"));

HashSet size with equals but no hashCode: 2
get after mutation: null | size: 1 | containsValue: true

Two “equal” objects land in different buckets, so the set holds both. And the mutated key is looked up in the bucket for "B" while the entry sits in the bucket for "A": the map still holds the value, but nothing can reach it by key. Make keys immutable. Java records and Scala case classes generate consistent equals and hashCode from final fields.

116. volatile vs synchronized vs AtomicLong vs LongAdder. 
static volatile int volatileCounter = 0;

AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong();
LongAdder adder = new LongAdder();
// 8 threads, each running 100,000 times:
volatileCounter++;            // read, add, write: three steps
atomic.incrementAndGet();     // one compare-and-swap loop
adder.increment();            // striped cells, summed on read

expected 800000 | volatile int: 455385 | AtomicLong: 800000 | LongAdder: 800000
  • volatile guarantees visibility: a write is seen by later reads in other threads. It does not make count++ atomic, and about 345,000 increments were lost.
  • synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility for a block. Correct, and it serializes the threads.
  • AtomicLong uses compare-and-swap for single-variable updates.
  • LongAdder spreads updates across cells and sums them on read. Under heavy contention it is faster than AtomicLong for counters, which is why metrics libraries use it.

The classic correct use of volatile is a stop flag that a worker loop reads.

117. Why does Spark throw "Task not serializable", and how do you fix it?

A closure sent to executors refers to an object that is not Serializable. The usual case: a lambda inside a class uses a field of that class, so the whole enclosing instance is captured. Reproduced in spark-shell:

class Enricher(val rate: Double) {           // not Serializable
  def run(df: Dataset[Long]) = df.map(x => x * rate)   // captures `this`
  def runSafe(df: Dataset[Long]) = {
    val r = rate                              // copy the field into a local
    df.map(x => x * r)
  }
}
val nums = spark.range(5).as[Long]
new Enricher(1.5).run(nums).collect()        // fails
new Enricher(1.5).runSafe(nums).collect()    // works

org.apache.spark.SparkException: Task not serializable
cause: java.io.NotSerializableException: $line14.$read$$iw$$iw$$iw$$iw$$iw$$iw$$iw$$iw$Enricher
local copy works: 0.0, 1.5, 3.0, 4.5, 6.0

The $line14.$read$$iw... prefix is the REPL’s wrapper class; in compiled code the message names your class directly. The fixes:

  • Copy the needed field into a local variable before the lambda, as runSafe does, so only a Double is captured.
  • Mark members that should not travel as transient, and create them lazily on the executor.
  • Create per-partition resources, such as a database connection, inside mapPartitions or foreachPartition, never on the driver.
  • Put helpers in a Scala object or a static method.

The “Serialization stack” in the exception lists the chain of fields that pulled the object in. Read it from the bottom.

118. Java Streams: lazy evaluation, and when parallelStream() is a bad idea. 
List<String> log = new ArrayList<>();
Stream<Integer> s = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
    .filter(x -> { log.add("filter " + x); return x % 2 == 0; })
    .map(x -> { log.add("map " + x); return x * 10; });
System.out.println("operations run before the terminal op: " + log.size());
System.out.println("findFirst -> " + s.findFirst().get() + " after " + log);

List<Integer> unsafe = new ArrayList<>();
IntStream.range(0, 100_000).parallel().forEach(unsafe::add);   // shared mutable state
List<Integer> safe = IntStream.range(0, 100_000).parallel().boxed().collect(Collectors.toList());
System.out.println("parallel forEach into ArrayList: " + unsafe.size() + " | collect(): " + safe.size());

operations run before the terminal op: 0
findFirst -> 20 after [filter 1, filter 2, map 2]
parallel forEach into ArrayList: 30947 | collect(): 100000

Nothing ran until findFirst, and then only three operations: elements flow through the whole pipeline one at a time, and evaluation stops at the first match. That is Spark’s transformations and actions (question 21) inside one JVM.

The parallel forEach into an ArrayList kept 30,947 of 100,000 elements; on another run it can throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead. Use collect(). parallelStream() also hurts when the source splits badly (a LinkedList, I/O), when per-element work is tiny, and inside a Spark task, where it competes with Spark’s own task threads for the executor’s cores.

119. Why are Strings immutable, == vs equals(), and when to use StringBuilder. 
String a = "data", b = "data", c = new String("data");
System.out.println("literal == literal: " + (a == b) + " | literal == new String: " + (a == c)
        + " | equals: " + a.equals(c));

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) sb.append(i).append(',');
System.out.println("StringBuilder: " + sb);

literal == literal: true | literal == new String: false | equals: true
StringBuilder: 0,1,2,3,4,

String literals are interned, so two literals are the same object; new String creates another. == compares references and equals compares content, so always compare strings with equals.

Strings are immutable so they can be shared safely between threads, cached in the intern pool, and used as HashMap keys whose hash never changes. The cost: s += x in a loop creates a new String every iteration, which is quadratic. Use a StringBuilder (not synchronized) inside a loop.

120. Call four sources in parallel and keep going if one fails, with CompletableFuture. 
ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
List<CompletableFuture<String>> calls = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 4)
    .mapToObj(i -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
        if (i == 3) throw new IllegalStateException("source " + i + " down");
        return "source " + i + " ok";
    }, io).exceptionally(e -> "fallback for " + e.getCause().getMessage()))
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

CompletableFuture.allOf(calls.toArray(new CompletableFuture[0])).get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
calls.forEach(f -> System.out.println(f.join()));
io.shutdown();

source 1 ok
source 2 ok
fallback for source 3 down
source 4 ok

supplyAsync runs each call on the pool, exceptionally turns a failure into a fallback value, and allOf(...).get(timeout) waits for all with an upper bound. Pass your own executor for I/O. The default common ForkJoinPool is sized for CPU work and is shared with parallel streams.

121. try-with-resources: in what order are resources closed, and what happens to the exception? 
final class Conn implements AutoCloseable {
    final String name;
    Conn(String name) { this.name = name; System.out.println("open " + name); }
    @Override public void close() { System.out.println("close " + name); }
}

try (Conn a = new Conn("source"); Conn b = new Conn("target")) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("copy failed");
} catch (IllegalStateException e) {
    System.out.println("caught: " + e.getMessage());
}

open source
open target
close target
close source
caught: copy failed

Resources close in reverse order of opening, and before the catch block runs. If close() itself throws, that exception is added to the original as a suppressed exception (e.getSuppressed()), so the real cause is not lost, which is what a hand-written finally usually gets wrong.

Scala

All of these ran in spark-shell on Spark 3.5.9 with Scala 2.12.

122. What does a case class give you, and why does Spark use them? 
case class Order(orderId: Long, customer: String, amount: Double)

val o1 = Order(1, "ranga", 250.0)
val o2 = o1.copy(amount = 300.0)
println(s"equal by value: ${o1 == Order(1, "ranga", 250.0)} | copy: $o2")
o2 match { case Order(id, c, amt) if amt > 100 => println(s"big order $id for $c") }

val ds = spark.read.parquet(path).as[Order]
def pushed(plan: String) = plan.linesIterator.find(_.contains("PushedFilters"))
  .map(_.split("PushedFilters: ")(1).takeWhile(_ != ']') + "]").getOrElse("none")
println("typed lambda  PushedFilters: " + pushed(ds.filter(_.amount > 100).queryExecution.executedPlan.toString))
println("column expr   PushedFilters: " + pushed(ds.filter($"amount" > 100).queryExecution.executedPlan.toString))

equal by value: true | copy: Order(1,ranga,300.0)
big order 1 for ranga
typed lambda  PushedFilters: []
column expr   PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(amount), GreaterThan(amount,100.0)]

A case class generates equals, hashCode and toString from its fields, a companion apply (no new), copy with named arguments, and unapply for pattern matching. Its fields are vals, so instances are immutable. Spark derives an Encoder for it, which gives a typed Dataset[Order].

The trap is in the plan: the typed lambda pushed no filters to the Parquet reader, because a Scala function is opaque to Catalyst. The column expression pushed both. Use typed lambdas where type safety matters more than pushdown, and columns on large scans.

123. val vs var vs lazy val vs def. 
var evaluations = 0
lazy val expensive = { evaluations += 1; 42 }
def recomputed = { evaluations += 1; 42 }

println(s"before access: $evaluations")
expensive; expensive
println(s"after two lazy val reads: $evaluations")
recomputed; recomputed
println(s"after two def calls: $evaluations")

before access: 0
after two lazy val reads: 1
after two def calls: 3
  • val: evaluated once, at definition; cannot be reassigned.
  • var: mutable. Avoid it in shared or Spark code.
  • lazy val: evaluated once, on first access, then cached. Initialization is thread-safe, at a small locking cost.
  • def: evaluated on every call.

A lazy val inside a Scala object is the standard way to create one expensive resource per executor JVM, such as an HTTP client, without serializing it from the driver (question 117).

124. Option vs null, and map vs flatMap vs a for-comprehension. 
case class User(id: Int, email: Option[String])
val users = Map(1 -> User(1, Some("Ranga@X.com")), 2 -> User(2, None))
def findUser(id: Int): Option[User] = users.get(id)

def emailOf(id: Int): Option[String] = for {
  user  <- findUser(id)          // Option[User]
  email <- user.email            // Option[String]
} yield email.toLowerCase

println(s"user 1: ${emailOf(1)} | user 2: ${emailOf(2)} | user 9: ${emailOf(9)}")
println(s"getOrElse: ${emailOf(2).getOrElse("unknown")} | Option(null): ${Option(null: String)}")
try { emailOf(2).get } catch { case e: NoSuchElementException => println("None.get -> NoSuchElementException") }

user 1: Some(ranga@x.com) | user 2: None | user 9: None
getOrElse: unknown | Option(null): None
None.get -> NoSuchElementException

Option[T] is Some(value) or None, so absence is part of the type. Option(x) turns a Java null into None. map transforms the value inside; flatMap is for functions that return an Option themselves, giving Option[B] instead of Option[Option[B]]. A for-comprehension is a chain of flatMap calls ending in map, and it short-circuits on the first None.

The trap: .get on None throws NoSuchElementException. Use getOrElse, fold or pattern matching.

125. Implicits in Scala 2 and given/using in Scala 3: what are they, and where does Spark rely on them? 
implicit class RichAmount(val amount: Double) {          // adds a method to Double
  def withTax(rate: Double = 0.18): Double =
    BigDecimal(amount * (1 + rate)).setScale(2, BigDecimal.RoundingMode.HALF_UP).toDouble
}
println(s"100.0.withTax() = ${100.0.withTax()}")

def fmt(x: Double)(implicit currency: String): String = s"$currency $x"
implicit val inr: String = "INR"                         // filled in by the compiler
println(fmt(250.0))

import spark.implicits._
println(s"encoder from spark.implicits._: ${implicitly[Encoder[Order]].schema.simpleString}")
println(s"Scala version: ${scala.util.Properties.versionString}")

100.0.withTax() = 118.0
INR 250.0
encoder from spark.implicits._: struct<orderId:bigint,customer:string,amount:double>
Scala version: version 2.12.18

An implicit parameter is filled in by the compiler from an implicit value in scope; an implicit class adds methods to an existing type. Scala 3 splits these uses apart: given instances with using parameters, and extension methods.

Spark depends on implicits through import spark.implicits._, which provides the Encoders behind toDF(), toDS() and as[T], and the $"col" syntax. Spark 3.5 is built for Scala 2.12 and 2.13 and Spark 4 for 2.13 only; neither publishes a Scala 3 build, so Spark code still uses Scala 2 implicits. Forget the import and the compiler says Unable to find encoder for type.

126. Trait vs abstract class, and which method wins when two traits override the same one. 
trait Step    { def run(x: Int): Int = x }
trait Double2 extends Step { override def run(x: Int): Int = super.run(x) * 2 }
trait Plus1   extends Step { override def run(x: Int): Int = super.run(x) + 1 }

class A extends Step with Double2 with Plus1
class B extends Step with Plus1 with Double2
println(s"Double2 then Plus1 (rightmost runs first): ${new A().run(5)} | Plus1 then Double2: ${new B().run(5)}")

Double2 then Plus1 (rightmost runs first): 11 | Plus1 then Double2: 12

Linearization: the rightmost trait’s method runs first, and its super.run calls the trait to its left. In A, Plus1 runs first and calls Double2, which calls Step: (5 × 2) + 1 = 11. In B it is (5 + 1) × 2 = 12.

A class can mix in many traits but extend one class. In Scala 2 a trait cannot take constructor parameters (Scala 3 allows it). Use a trait for a capability that mixes into many types (logging, retry, metrics); use an abstract class for a base type that needs constructor arguments or must be called from Java.

127. Write a tail-recursive function, and say what @tailrec guarantees. 
import scala.annotation.tailrec

def sum(xs: List[Long]): Long = {
  @tailrec
  def loop(rest: List[Long], acc: Long): Long = rest match {
    case Nil    => acc
    case h :: t => loop(t, acc + h)       // the recursive call is the last action
  }
  loop(xs, 0L)
}
def sumNaive(xs: List[Long]): Long = xs match { case Nil => 0L; case h :: t => h + sumNaive(t) }

val big = List.range(1L, 1000001L)
println(s"tail-recursive sum of 1..1,000,000 = ${sum(big)} | foldLeft = ${big.foldLeft(0L)(_ + _)}")
try { sumNaive(big) }                      // h + ... is not a tail call
catch { case _: StackOverflowError => println("non-tail-recursive version -> StackOverflowError") }

tail-recursive sum of 1..1,000,000 = 500000500000 | foldLeft = 500000500000
non-tail-recursive version -> StackOverflowError

A call in tail position is compiled into a loop, so the stack does not grow. sumNaive adds h after the recursive call returns, so every element needs a stack frame, and a million elements overflow the stack.

@tailrec does not create the optimization. It makes the compiler fail if the call is not in tail position, so a later edit cannot quietly bring back a StackOverflowError. In practice, foldLeft does the same job in one line.

Spark

128. What does Adaptive Query Execution change at runtime?

AQE re-plans a query between stages, using the real sizes of the shuffle output instead of estimates. It is on by default since Spark 3.2 and does three things:

  1. Coalesces shuffle partitions. 200 tiny post-shuffle partitions become a few right-sized ones.
  2. Switches join strategy. A sort-merge join becomes a broadcast join when one side turns out small after filtering.
  3. Splits skewed partitions in joins (question 31).

The first one, measured on a 10-key aggregation:

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
d = spark.range(0, 100_000).groupBy((F.col("id") % 10).alias("k")).count()
d.collect()
print("final plan partitions:", d.rdd.getNumPartitions())

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false")
d2 = spark.range(0, 100_000).groupBy((F.col("id") % 10).alias("k")).count()
print("without AQE:", d2.rdd.getNumPartitions())

final plan partitions: 1
without AQE: 200

Without AQE the result has 200 partitions for 10 rows, which means 200 tasks and, if written, 200 files. With AQE, one.

In explain() output, an AQE plan starts with AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false before it runs. Look at the SQL tab in the Spark UI after it runs for the final plan, where coalesced reads show as AQEShuffleRead.

129. A file has malformed records. How does Spark handle them, and how do you keep them instead of losing them?

Three read modes, one bad file with a type error on line 2 and a truncated record on line 3:

with open(bad, "w") as fh:
    fh.write('{"id": 1, "amount": 10.5}\n{"id": 2, "amount": "oops"}\n{"id": 3, "amount": 7.0\n')

schema = "id INT, amount DOUBLE, _corrupt_record STRING"
(spark.read.schema(schema).option("mode", "PERMISSIVE")
      .option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_corrupt_record").json(bad)).show(truncate=False)

spark.read.schema("id INT, amount DOUBLE").option("mode", "DROPMALFORMED").json(bad).count()

spark.read.schema("id INT, amount DOUBLE").option("mode", "FAILFAST").json(bad).collect()

PERMISSIVE:
+----+------+---------------------------+
|id  |amount|_corrupt_record            |
+----+------+---------------------------+
|1   |10.5  |NULL                       |
|2   |NULL  |{"id": 2, "amount": "oops"}|
|NULL|NULL  |{"id": 3, "amount": 7.0    |
+----+------+---------------------------+

DROPMALFORMED count: 2
org.apache.spark.SparkException: [MALFORMED_RECORD_IN_PARSING.WITHOUT_SUGGESTION] Malformed records are detected in record parsing: [2,null].
  • PERMISSIVE (the default) keeps every row, sets unparseable fields to NULL, and puts the raw text in the corrupt-record column, if the schema declares one.
  • DROPMALFORMED silently drops bad rows. Two of three survived here, and nothing says so.
  • FAILFAST throws SparkException: [MALFORMED_RECORD_IN_PARSING.WITHOUT_SUGGESTION] on the first bad record.

For a pipeline, use PERMISSIVE with the corrupt-record column, write rows where it is not null to a quarantine table, and alert on the count. One trap: since Spark 2.3, a query that references only the corrupt-record column of a raw JSON or CSV file is rejected. Cache or save the parsed DataFrame first, then filter on it.

PySpark practice set

Coding rounds for Spark-heavy teams tend to draw from the same pool: write a MERGE that survives retries, sessionize clicks, flatten JSON, beat skew, check data quality. One problem below points to answers earlier in the post; the rest are answered here. Each one ran on Spark 3.5.9 with Delta Lake 3.3.2, and the code shown is what produced the output under it.

Problem Skills it exercises Answered in
Upsert customer profiles so a retry is harmless MERGE, a version guard, in-batch dedup Q130
Turn reading-app screens into sessions lag, a running sum, session_window Q131
Flatten trip events with nested lists explode_outer, struct paths, from_json Q132
One tenant sends 90% of the traffic Two-step salted aggregation Q133 (salted joins: Q31)

Validate invoices against configurable rules A rule registry, a report, a release gate Q134
Keep history for a product dimension SCD Type 2 with plain DataFrames Q135 (with MERGE: Q51)

130. Write an upsert for customer profiles that is safe to retry: repeated keys in a batch, stale changes, and replays.

A Delta MERGE keyed on the customer does the inserting and updating. Three additions make it safe to run again and again:

profiles = f"file://{BASE}/profiles"
spark.createDataFrame([
    ("CU-9", "vinod@x.com", "free", "2026-10-20 08:00:00"),
    ("CU-7", "yashu@x.com", "pro",  "2026-10-21 12:00:00"),
], "customer_id STRING, email STRING, plan STRING, updated_at STRING") \
    .withColumn("updated_at", F.to_timestamp("updated_at")).write.format("delta").save(profiles)

def upsert(batch, path, key="customer_id", version_col="updated_at"):
    """Safe to retry: a replayed batch, or an older version of a row, changes nothing."""
    newest = dedup_latest(batch, [key], [F.col(version_col).desc()])          # one row per key
    (DeltaTable.forPath(spark, path).alias("t")
       .merge(newest.alias("s"), f"t.{key} = s.{key}")
       .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition=f"s.{version_col} > t.{version_col}")  # newer only
       .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
       .execute())

changes = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("CU-9", "vinod@x.com",     "pro",   "2026-10-22 09:00:00"),
    ("CU-9", "vinod.k@x.com",   "pro",   "2026-10-22 18:00:00"),   # the same customer twice
    ("CU-7", "yashu@x.com",     "free",  "2026-10-19 10:00:00"),   # older than what we hold
    ("CU-3", "lakshmi@x.com",   "team",  "2026-10-22 11:00:00"),   # new
], "customer_id STRING, email STRING, plan STRING, updated_at STRING") \
    .withColumn("updated_at", F.to_timestamp("updated_at"))

upsert(changes, profiles)
first = spark.read.format("delta").load(profiles).orderBy("customer_id").collect()
upsert(changes, profiles)                                               # the retry
second = spark.read.format("delta").load(profiles).orderBy("customer_id").collect()
spark.read.format("delta").load(profiles).orderBy("customer_id").show()
print("same table after applying the batch twice:", first == second)
try:
    (DeltaTable.forPath(spark, profiles).alias("t").merge(changes.alias("s"), "t.customer_id = s.customer_id")
       .whenMatchedUpdateAll().whenNotMatchedInsertAll().execute())
except Exception as e:
    print("MERGE straight from the raw batch:", type(e).__name__, "-", str(e).splitlines()[0][:110])

+-----------+-------------+----+-------------------+
|customer_id|        email|plan|         updated_at|
+-----------+-------------+----+-------------------+
|       CU-3|lakshmi@x.com|team|2026-10-22 11:00:00|
|       CU-7|  yashu@x.com| pro|2026-10-21 12:00:00|
|       CU-9|vinod.k@x.com| pro|2026-10-22 18:00:00|
+-----------+-------------+----+-------------------+

same table after applying the batch twice: True
MERGE straight from the raw batch: UnsupportedOperationException - [DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE] Cannot perform Merge as multiple source rows matched
  • A key repeated within the batch. CU-9 changed twice. Delta refuses to apply two source rows to one target row, and the last line shows the error you get (DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE). Reducing the batch to the newest row per key first (dedup_latest, question 137) keeps the 18:00 change.
  • A change older than the table. CU-7’s incoming row is from 19 October, but the table already holds the 21 October version. The s.updated_at > t.updated_at guard ignores it, so a delayed message cannot undo a newer one.
  • A replay. Applying the same batch a second time leaves the table identical.

On a large partitioned table, add the partition column to the join condition so the MERGE reads only the partitions the batch touches.

131. Turn a reading app's screen views into sessions: a new session after more than 30 idle minutes.

Same logic as the SQL answer (question 76): minutes since the previous view with lag, a 1 where a session starts, and a running sum of those 1s as the session number. Spark also offers session_window:

reads = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("anada", "2026-10-03 08:15:00", "home"), ("anada", "2026-10-03 08:20:00", "chapter-1"),
    ("anada", "2026-10-03 08:44:00", "chapter-2"), ("anada", "2026-10-03 09:20:00", "home"),
    ("anada", "2026-10-03 09:21:00", "chapter-3"),
    ("lakshmi", "2026-10-03 21:00:00", "home"), ("lakshmi", "2026-10-03 21:30:00", "chapter-9"),  # 30 min exactly
], "user_id STRING, ts STRING, screen STRING").withColumn("ts", F.to_timestamp("ts"))

by_user = Window.partitionBy("user_id").orderBy("ts")
minutes_idle = (F.col("ts").cast("long") - F.lag("ts").over(by_user).cast("long")) / 60
sessions = (reads
            .withColumn("idle_min", minutes_idle)
            .withColumn("starts", F.when(F.col("idle_min").isNull() | (F.col("idle_min") > 30), 1).otherwise(0))
            .withColumn("session_no", F.sum("starts").over(by_user.rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, 0)))
            .withColumn("session_id", F.concat_ws("#", "user_id", "session_no")))
sessions.orderBy("user_id", "ts").show()

print("the same with session_window:")
(reads.groupBy("user_id", F.session_window("ts", "30 minutes"))
      .agg(F.count("*").alias("screens"))
      .select("user_id", "session_window.start", "session_window.end", "screens")
      .orderBy("user_id", "start").show(truncate=False))

+-------+-------------------+---------+--------+------+----------+----------+
|user_id|                 ts|   screen|idle_min|starts|session_no|session_id|
+-------+-------------------+---------+--------+------+----------+----------+
|  anada|2026-10-03 08:15:00|     home|    NULL|     1|         1|   anada#1|
|  anada|2026-10-03 08:20:00|chapter-1|     5.0|     0|         1|   anada#1|
|  anada|2026-10-03 08:44:00|chapter-2|    24.0|     0|         1|   anada#1|
|  anada|2026-10-03 09:20:00|     home|    36.0|     1|         2|   anada#2|
|  anada|2026-10-03 09:21:00|chapter-3|     1.0|     0|         2|   anada#2|
|lakshmi|2026-10-03 21:00:00|     home|    NULL|     1|         1| lakshmi#1|
|lakshmi|2026-10-03 21:30:00|chapter-9|    30.0|     0|         1| lakshmi#1|
+-------+-------------------+---------+--------+------+----------+----------+

the same with session_window:
+-------+-------------------+-------------------+-------+
|user_id|start              |end                |screens|
+-------+-------------------+-------------------+-------+
|anada  |2026-10-03 08:15:00|2026-10-03 09:14:00|3      |
|anada  |2026-10-03 09:20:00|2026-10-03 09:51:00|2      |
|lakshmi|2026-10-03 21:00:00|2026-10-03 22:00:00|2      |
+-------+-------------------+-------------------+-------+

Anada was idle for 36 minutes before 09:20, so session 2 begins there. Lakshmi’s second screen is exactly 30 minutes after her first, and the rule is “more than 30”, so it stays in session 1.

Notice the end column from session_window: it is the last event plus the 30-minute gap (08:44 becomes 09:14), not the last event itself. Window functions are the choice when every row needs its session id; session_window is the choice for per-session totals, and it also runs in Structured Streaming with a watermark.

132. Flatten trip events: a nested rider object, a list of stops that each carry a list of tags, and fare details stored as a JSON string.

Nested objects and lists need different tools. A nested object is just a path (rider.home.city) and never changes how many rows you have. A list needs explode, which adds a row per element. A JSON string needs from_json with a schema before either applies. The three trips cover the awkward cases: an empty stop list, a missing stop list, a missing home address and an unparseable fare:

trips_json = f"{BASE}/trips.json"
with open(trips_json, "w") as fh:
    for t in [
        {"trip_id": "T1", "rider": {"name": "Anada", "home": {"city": "Mysuru"}},
         "stops": [{"seq": 1, "place": "Airport", "tags": ["pickup", "toll"]},
                   {"seq": 2, "place": "Palace", "tags": []}],
         "fare": '{"currency": "INR", "total": 640.0}'},
        {"trip_id": "T2", "rider": {"name": "Lakshmi", "home": None},
         "stops": [], "fare": '{"currency": "INR", "total": 85.0}'},          # empty list
        {"trip_id": "T3", "rider": {"name": "Manoj", "home": {"city": "Kochi"}},
         "stops": None, "fare": "{broken"},                                   # null list, bad JSON
    ]:
        fh.write(json.dumps(t) + "\n")

raw = spark.read.json(trips_json)
raw.printSchema()

fare_schema = StructType([StructField("currency", StringType()), StructField("total", DoubleType())])

flat = (raw
        .withColumn("stop", F.explode_outer("stops"))            # a row per stop; keeps T2 and T3
        .withColumn("tag", F.explode_outer("stop.tags"))         # a list inside a list: explode again
        .withColumn("fare", F.from_json("fare", fare_schema))    # unparseable text becomes null
        .select("trip_id",
                F.col("rider.name").alias("rider"),             # nested objects: just a path
                F.col("rider.home.city").alias("home_city"),
                F.col("stop.seq").alias("stop_seq"),
                F.col("stop.place").alias("place"),
                "tag",
                F.col("fare.total").alias("fare_total")))
flat.orderBy("trip_id", "stop_seq", "tag").show()
print("stop rows with explode:", raw.select(F.explode("stops")).count(),
      "| with explode_outer:", raw.select(F.explode_outer("stops")).count())

root
 |-- fare: string (nullable = true)
 |-- rider: struct (nullable = true)
 |    |-- home: struct (nullable = true)
 |    |    |-- city: string (nullable = true)
 |    |-- name: string (nullable = true)
 |-- stops: array (nullable = true)
 |    |-- element: struct (containsNull = true)
 |    |    |-- place: string (nullable = true)
 |    |    |-- seq: long (nullable = true)
 |    |    |-- tags: array (nullable = true)
 |    |    |    |-- element: string (containsNull = true)
 |-- trip_id: string (nullable = true)

+-------+-------+---------+--------+-------+------+----------+
|trip_id|  rider|home_city|stop_seq|  place|   tag|fare_total|
+-------+-------+---------+--------+-------+------+----------+
|     T1|  Anada|   Mysuru|       1|Airport|pickup|     640.0|
|     T1|  Anada|   Mysuru|       1|Airport|  toll|     640.0|
|     T1|  Anada|   Mysuru|       2| Palace|  NULL|     640.0|
|     T2|Lakshmi|     NULL|    NULL|   NULL|  NULL|      85.0|
|     T3|  Manoj|    Kochi|    NULL|   NULL|  NULL|      NULL|
+-------+-------+---------+--------+-------+------+----------+

stop rows with explode: 2 | with explode_outer: 4
  • explode versus explode_outer. With plain explode, trips T2 and T3 vanish (2 stop rows instead of 4), because an empty or null list produces no rows. explode_outer keeps them with nulls.
  • Row counts multiply. T1 has two stops and the first has two tags, so T1 becomes three rows, and fare_total is repeated on all of them. Sum trip-level values before exploding, or the total triples.
  • Bad JSON turns into nulls, silently. T3’s fare could not be parsed, and nothing failed. Count those nulls if they matter.

Declare schemas in production rather than relying on inference, so a new or changed field is something you decided, not something you discover.

133. One tenant sends 90% of all requests. Compute per-tenant counts and average latency without one task doing all the work.

A groupBy sends every row of a tenant to one task, so the big tenant becomes one very slow task. Spread it out in two steps: add a random bucket number, aggregate per tenant and bucket, then combine the buckets:

requests = (spark.range(0, 1_000_000)
            .withColumn("tenant", F.when(F.col("id") % 10 < 9, F.lit("acme"))           # one tenant: 90%
                                   .otherwise(F.concat(F.lit("t"), (F.col("id") % 300).cast("string"))))
            .withColumn("latency_ms", (F.col("id") % 389).cast("double")))
BUCKETS = 12

per_bucket = (requests
              .withColumn("bucket", (F.rand(17) * BUCKETS).cast("int"))
              .groupBy("tenant", "bucket")                            # step 1: the big tenant split 12 ways
              .agg(F.count("*").alias("n"), F.sum("latency_ms").alias("sum_ms")))
per_tenant = (per_bucket.groupBy("tenant")                            # step 2: combine the small partials
              .agg(F.sum("n").alias("requests"), F.sum("sum_ms").alias("sum_ms"))
              .withColumn("avg_ms", F.col("sum_ms") / F.col("requests")))

direct = requests.groupBy("tenant").agg(F.count("*").alias("requests"), F.avg("latency_ms").alias("avg_ms"))
mismatches = per_tenant.join(direct, "tenant").filter(
    (per_tenant.requests != direct.requests) | (F.abs(per_tenant.avg_ms - direct.avg_ms) > 1e-9)).count()
print("tenants:", per_tenant.count(), "| tenants that differ from a direct groupBy:", mismatches)
per_tenant.filter("tenant = 'acme'").select("tenant", "requests", F.round("avg_ms", 3).alias("avg_ms")).show()

rows_per_task = lambda df, cols: sorted(df.repartition(8, *cols).rdd.glom().map(len).collect(), reverse=True)
bucketed = requests.withColumn("bucket", (F.rand(17) * BUCKETS).cast("int"))
print("rows per shuffle partition, by tenant         :", rows_per_task(requests, ["tenant"]))
print("rows per shuffle partition, by tenant + bucket:", rows_per_task(bucketed, ["tenant", "bucket"]))

tenants: 31 | tenants that differ from a direct groupBy: 0
+------+--------+-------+
|tenant|requests| avg_ms|
+------+--------+-------+
|  acme|  900000|193.984|
+------+--------+-------+

rows per shuffle partition, by tenant         : [906666, 30002, 20001, 13333, 10000, 9999, 6666, 3333]
rows per shuffle partition, by tenant + bucket: [313289, 236779, 235586, 89404, 86843, 14520, 13609, 9970]
  • Same answer: none of the 31 tenants differs from a direct groupBy, averages included.
  • Smaller worst task: the largest shuffle partition falls from 906,666 rows to about 313,000. It is not 12 equal pieces, because 12 buckets hash into only 8 partitions and some collide; more buckets or more partitions even it out further.
  • Only combinable measures split this way. Counts and sums combine across buckets, so the average is rebuilt as total ÷ count. An average of bucket averages would be wrong, and medians or exact distinct counts cannot be combined like this at all; use percentile_approx or a sketch (question 55).

AQE’s skew handling (question 31) splits oversized partitions in joins only, which is why aggregations still need this by hand.

134. Validate invoices against rules kept in configuration, report every result, and block the release on serious failures.

The checks themselves are simple; the design is the point. The rules are a list that could live in YAML or a table, each check type is one function, and a dictionary connects the two, so supporting a new kind of rule never touches the runner:

invoices = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("INV-7001", "V-1", 1200.0, "INR"),
    ("INV-7002", "V-2",  480.0, "INR"),
    ("INV-7003", None,   310.0, "INR"),
    ("INV-7002", "V-2",  480.0, "INR"),
    ("INV-7004", "V-1",    0.0, "USD"),
    ("INV-7005", "V-9",   75.0, "YEN"),
], "invoice_id STRING, vendor_id STRING, total DOUBLE, currency STRING")
vendors = spark.createDataFrame([("V-1",), ("V-2",), ("V-3",)], "vendor_id STRING")

RULES = [   # configuration: load from YAML or a table in a real job
    {"name": "invoice_id present",  "check": "not_null", "column": "invoice_id", "severity": "block"},
    {"name": "vendor_id present",   "check": "not_null", "column": "vendor_id",  "severity": "block"},
    {"name": "invoice_id unique",   "check": "unique",   "column": "invoice_id", "severity": "block"},
    {"name": "total above zero",    "check": "min_exclusive", "column": "total", "min": 0, "severity": "block"},
    {"name": "known currency",      "check": "allowed",  "column": "currency",
     "values": ["INR", "USD", "EUR"], "severity": "warn"},
    {"name": "vendor on file",      "check": "lookup",   "column": "vendor_id",
     "ref": vendors, "ref_column": "vendor_id", "severity": "warn"},
]

def check_not_null(df, r):  return df.filter(F.col(r["column"]).isNull()).count()
def check_unique(df, r):    return df.groupBy(r["column"]).count().filter("count > 1").agg(F.coalesce(F.sum("count"), F.lit(0))).first()[0]
def check_min(df, r):       return df.filter(F.col(r["column"]) <= r["min"]).count()
def check_allowed(df, r):   return df.filter(~F.col(r["column"]).isin(r["values"])).count()
def check_lookup(df, r):
    present = df.filter(F.col(r["column"]).isNotNull())
    return present.join(r["ref"], present[r["column"]] == r["ref"][r["ref_column"]], "left_anti").count()

CHECKS = {"not_null": check_not_null, "unique": check_unique, "min_exclusive": check_min,
          "allowed": check_allowed, "lookup": check_lookup}       # adding a check type: one line here

def evaluate(df, rules):
    rows = df.count()
    results = [(r["name"], r["severity"], CHECKS[r["check"]](df, r), rows) for r in rules]
    return (spark.createDataFrame(results, "rule STRING, severity STRING, bad_rows LONG, rows LONG")
                 .withColumn("ok", F.col("bad_rows") == 0))

report = evaluate(invoices, RULES)
report.show(truncate=False)
blocking = report.filter("NOT ok AND severity = 'block'").count()
print("blocking failures:", blocking, "-> do not publish" if blocking else "-> publish")

+------------------+--------+--------+----+-----+
|rule              |severity|bad_rows|rows|ok   |
+------------------+--------+--------+----+-----+
|invoice_id present|block   |0       |6   |true |
|vendor_id present |block   |1       |6   |false|
|invoice_id unique |block   |2       |6   |false|
|total above zero  |block   |1       |6   |false|
|known currency    |warn    |1       |6   |false|
|vendor on file    |warn    |1       |6   |false|
+------------------+--------+--------+----+-----+

blocking failures: 3 -> do not publish

Six invoices, five failed rules: one missing vendor, one invoice number used twice (both copies counted, so 2), a zero total, an unrecognised currency, and a vendor that is not on file. Severity decides what happens next: block failures stop the release, warn failures are reported and alerted on.

Worth saying in an interview: each rule here is a separate Spark job, so fold the counts into one aggregation pass when the rule list grows; store every report with its run id to see trends; and tools like Great Expectations or Deequ package the same idea.

135. Keep history for a product dimension with plain DataFrames: expire changed rows, add new versions, and handle two changes on one day.

Question 51 does Type 2 with a Delta MERGE. Without one, rebuild the dimension from four pieces: rows that stay as they are, rows that expire today, new versions of changed products, and brand-new products. A fingerprint of the tracked columns tells changed from unchanged:

dim = spark.createDataFrame([
    (101, "P-10", "Kettle",  "Kitchen", "2025-06-01", None, True),
    (102, "P-20", "Lantern", "Outdoor", "2025-08-20", None, True),
], "product_sk INT, product_id STRING, name STRING, category STRING, valid_from STRING, valid_to STRING, is_current BOOLEAN") \
    .withColumn("valid_from", F.to_date("valid_from")).withColumn("valid_to", F.to_date("valid_to"))

incoming = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("P-10", "Kettle",  "Appliances",    "2026-10-27 08:00:00"),
    ("P-10", "Kettle",  "Small appliances", "2026-10-27 17:30:00"),   # re-categorised twice today
    ("P-20", "Lantern", "Outdoor",       "2026-10-27 09:00:00"),      # no change
    ("P-30", "Hammock", "Outdoor",       "2026-10-27 10:00:00"),      # brand new
], "product_id STRING, name STRING, category STRING, changed_at STRING").withColumn("changed_at", F.to_timestamp("changed_at"))

TRACKED = ["name", "category"]                                 # only these create a new version
fingerprint = F.sha2(F.concat_ws("||", *[F.coalesce(F.col(c), F.lit("<null>")) for c in TRACKED]), 256)
as_of = F.to_date(F.lit("2026-10-27"))

today = dedup_latest(incoming, ["product_id"], [F.col("changed_at").desc()]).withColumn("fp", fingerprint)
live = dim.filter("is_current").withColumn("fp", fingerprint)

cmp = today.alias("n").join(live.alias("o"), "product_id", "left")
changed = cmp.filter("o.product_sk IS NOT NULL AND n.fp <> o.fp")
added = cmp.filter("o.product_sk IS NULL")

expired = (dim.join(changed.select("product_id"), "product_id", "left_semi")
              .filter("is_current")
              .withColumn("valid_to", as_of).withColumn("is_current", F.lit(False)))
kept = dim.join(expired.select("product_sk"), "product_sk", "left_anti")
next_sk = dim.agg(F.max("product_sk")).first()[0]
fresh = (changed.select("product_id", "n.name", "n.category").unionByName(added.select("product_id", "n.name", "n.category"))
         .withColumn("product_sk", F.lit(next_sk) + F.row_number().over(Window.orderBy("product_id")))
         .withColumn("valid_from", as_of)
         .withColumn("valid_to", F.lit(None).cast("date"))
         .withColumn("is_current", F.lit(True)))

kept.unionByName(expired).unionByName(fresh).orderBy("product_id", "valid_from").show()

+----------+----------+-------+----------------+----------+----------+----------+
|product_sk|product_id|   name|        category|valid_from|  valid_to|is_current|
+----------+----------+-------+----------------+----------+----------+----------+
|       101|      P-10| Kettle|         Kitchen|2025-06-01|2026-10-27|     false|
|       103|      P-10| Kettle|Small appliances|2026-10-27|      NULL|      true|
|       102|      P-20|Lantern|         Outdoor|2025-08-20|      NULL|      true|
|       104|      P-30|Hammock|         Outdoor|2026-10-27|      NULL|      true|
+----------+----------+-------+----------------+----------+----------+----------+
  • P-10 was re-categorised twice today. Only the latest change survives the per-key reduction, so “Small appliances” becomes the new version and “Appliances” never appears. Whether every intra-day change deserves its own version is a question for the business.
  • P-20 did not change, so its fingerprint matches and its row is untouched.
  • P-30 is new and receives the next surrogate key.
  • The fingerprint covers tracked columns only. Including something like a load timestamp would create a new version on every run.

Rebuilding the whole dimension is fine at thousands or millions of rows; beyond that, MERGE (question 51) rewrites only the files holding changed products.

136. Count page views per country in 10-minute windows, accept events up to 15 minutes late, and write each window to Delta once.

Question 40 shows watermarks with a memory sink; this is the production shape: a declared schema, a watermark, tumbling windows, append mode into Delta and a checkpoint. A folder of JSON files stands in for Kafka (question 38 reads Kafka), and maxFilesPerTrigger turns each file into its own micro-batch:

src, out, chk = f"{BASE}/views_in", f"file://{BASE}/views_10min", f"{BASE}/chk_views"
os.makedirs(src)
schema = StructType([StructField("country", StringType()), StructField("views", DoubleType()),
                     StructField("event_time", TimestampType())])

def land(name, rows):
    with open(f"{src}/{name}.json", "w") as fh:
        fh.writelines(json.dumps(r) + "\n" for r in rows)

def run_stream():
    agg = (spark.readStream.schema(schema).option("maxFilesPerTrigger", 1).json(src)   # schema is declared
           .withWatermark("event_time", "15 minutes")
           .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 minutes"), "country")
           .agg(F.count("*").alias("events"), F.sum("views").alias("views")))
    q = (agg.writeStream.format("delta").outputMode("append")
         .option("checkpointLocation", chk)            # progress and state survive restarts
         .trigger(availableNow=True).start(out))
    q.awaitTermination()
    return spark.read.format("delta").load(out).select("window.start", "country", "events", "views") \
                .orderBy("start", "country")

land("a", [{"country": "IN", "views": 3.0, "event_time": "2026-10-09T18:01:00"},
           {"country": "IN", "views": 1.0, "event_time": "2026-10-09T18:07:00"},
           {"country": "SG", "views": 2.0, "event_time": "2026-10-09T18:09:00"}])
land("b", [{"country": "IN", "views": 4.0, "event_time": "2026-10-09T18:33:00"}])
print("after the first run:"); run_stream().show(truncate=False)
land("c", [{"country": "IN", "views": 50.0, "event_time": "2026-10-09T18:05:00"},   # 28 minutes late
           {"country": "SG", "views": 1.0,  "event_time": "2026-10-09T19:02:00"}])
print("after the second run:"); run_stream().show(truncate=False)

after the first run:
+-------------------+-------+------+-----+
|start              |country|events|views|
+-------------------+-------+------+-----+
|2026-10-09 18:00:00|IN     |2     |4.0  |
|2026-10-09 18:00:00|SG     |1     |2.0  |
+-------------------+-------+------+-----+

after the second run:
+-------------------+-------+------+-----+
|start              |country|events|views|
+-------------------+-------+------+-----+
|2026-10-09 18:00:00|IN     |2     |4.0  |
|2026-10-09 18:00:00|SG     |1     |2.0  |
|2026-10-09 18:30:00|IN     |1     |4.0  |
+-------------------+-------+------+-----+

First run. The 18:33 event pushed the watermark to 18:18, which closed the 18:00-18:10 windows, so they were written. Nothing later had closed yet.

Second run. An Indian event from 18:05 arrived 28 minutes late. Its window was already closed and written, so the event was dropped and the table still shows 4.0 views, not 54.0. The 19:02 event moved the watermark to 18:47, which closed and wrote the 18:30 window; Singapore’s 19:00 window is still open.

The trade-off of append mode: every window is written once and never revised, but only after the watermark passes it, so results lag by the window length plus the allowed lateness. update mode publishes earlier, partial numbers, and then needs a sink that can overwrite them, typically a MERGE inside foreachBatch. The checkpoint plus Delta’s per-batch commit is what makes the output exactly-once.

137. Keep the latest scan for each shipment at each warehouse, and explain why dropDuplicates is not enough.

Partition by the key, order by recency, keep row 1. Written once as a function, it is reused by the upsert and SCD answers above:

scans = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("SHP-41", "BLR", "picked",     "2026-10-12 08:10:00", 7),
    ("SHP-41", "BLR", "packed",     "2026-10-12 09:45:00", 8),    # the later scan wins
    ("SHP-41", "HYD", "in_transit", "2026-10-12 21:00:00", 9),    # another warehouse: its own key
    ("SHP-52", "BLR", "packed",     "2026-10-12 11:30:00", 3),
    ("SHP-52", "BLR", "on_hold",    "2026-10-12 11:30:00", 4),    # same second: the scanner sequence decides
    (None,     "BLR", "picked",     "2026-10-12 12:00:00", 5),    # no shipment id
], "shipment_id STRING, warehouse STRING, status STRING, scanned_at STRING, scanner_seq INT") \
    .withColumn("scanned_at", F.to_timestamp("scanned_at"))

def dedup_latest(df, keys, order_by):
    """One row per key, the first by `order_by`. Make order_by unique per key, or ties are arbitrary."""
    w = Window.partitionBy(*keys).orderBy(*order_by)
    return (df.withColumn("_rn", F.row_number().over(w))
              .filter("_rn = 1").drop("_rn"))

current = dedup_latest(scans, ["shipment_id", "warehouse"],
                       [F.col("scanned_at").desc(), F.col("scanner_seq").desc()])
current.orderBy("shipment_id", "warehouse").show()
print("dropDuplicates on the same key also leaves", scans.dropDuplicates(["shipment_id", "warehouse"]).count(),
      "rows, with no rule for which one")

+-----------+---------+----------+-------------------+-----------+
|shipment_id|warehouse|    status|         scanned_at|scanner_seq|
+-----------+---------+----------+-------------------+-----------+
|       NULL|      BLR|    picked|2026-10-12 12:00:00|          5|
|     SHP-41|      BLR|    packed|2026-10-12 09:45:00|          8|
|     SHP-41|      HYD|in_transit|2026-10-12 21:00:00|          9|
|     SHP-52|      BLR|   on_hold|2026-10-12 11:30:00|          4|
+-----------+---------+----------+-------------------+-----------+

dropDuplicates on the same key also leaves 4 rows, with no rule for which one
  • SHP-41 has two scans at Bengaluru; the later one, packed, wins. Its Hyderabad scan is a different key, so it stays.
  • SHP-52’s two scans have the same timestamp; scanner_seq breaks the tie, so the result is the same on every run. Without a tiebreaker the winner is whichever row Spark happens to see first.
  • The scan with no shipment id forms its own group, because nulls are grouped together. Decide whether to keep it or send it to a rejects table.

dropDuplicates(["shipment_id", "warehouse"]) also returns 4 rows, but makes no promise about which row survives, so it can change between runs. It is fine for rows that are identical in every column, and wrong for “keep the latest”.

138. Write a meter-reading loader you could leave running overnight: settings, structured logs, a rejects table, retries and a safe write.

This one brings the earlier answers together, reusing upsert from question 130:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Settings:
    source: str
    target: str
    rejects: str
    business_date: str
    statuses: tuple = ("ok", "estimated")
    reject_limit: float = 0.3
    write_attempts: int = 3

log = logging.getLogger("meter_loader")
handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(message)s"))
log.addHandler(handler); log.setLevel(logging.INFO); log.propagate = False

def emit(step, **fields):                          # one JSON object per step: easy to query later
    log.info(json.dumps({"step": step, **fields}, sort_keys=True))

def retried(attempts, wait_s=0.2, on=(Exception,)):
    def deco(fn):
        @wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*a, **kw):
            for n in range(1, attempts + 1):
                try:
                    return fn(*a, **kw)
                except on as e:
                    emit("retry", fn=fn.__name__, attempt=n, error=type(e).__name__)
                    if n == attempts:
                        raise
                    time.sleep(wait_s * 2 ** (n - 1))
        return wrapper
    return deco

class Transient(Exception):
    pass

hiccups = {"left": 1}                              # the first write attempt fails, as if a node was lost

@retried(attempts=3, on=(Transient,))
def write_readings(df, s):
    if hiccups["left"]:
        hiccups["left"] -= 1
        raise Transient("storage timeout")
    upsert(df, s.target, key="meter_id", version_col="read_at")

def run(s):
    t0 = time.time()
    raw = spark.read.schema("meter_id STRING, kwh STRING, status STRING, read_at STRING, _bad_line STRING") \
               .option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_bad_line").json(s.source).cache()
    emit("read", rows=raw.count(), business_date=s.business_date)

    typed = raw.withColumn("kwh_num", F.col("kwh").cast("double")).withColumn("read_at", F.to_timestamp("read_at"))
    why = (F.when(F.col("_bad_line").isNotNull(), "unparseable_line")
            .when(F.col("meter_id").isNull(), "no_meter_id")
            .when(F.col("kwh_num").isNull(), "kwh_not_numeric")
            .when(F.col("kwh_num") < 0, "negative_kwh")
            .when(~F.col("status").isin(*s.statuses), "unknown_status"))
    tagged = typed.withColumn("why", why)
    good = tagged.filter("why IS NULL").select("meter_id", F.col("kwh_num").alias("kwh"), "status", "read_at")
    bad = tagged.filter("why IS NOT NULL")
    n_good, n_bad = good.count(), bad.count()
    emit("validate", accepted=n_good, rejected=n_bad,
         by_reason={r["why"]: r["count"] for r in bad.groupBy("why").count().collect()})

    (bad.select(F.lit(s.business_date).alias("business_date"), "why",            # raw kept for replay
                F.to_json(F.struct(*[c for c in raw.columns if c != "_bad_line"])).alias("raw"), "_bad_line")
        .write.format("delta").mode("overwrite")
        .option("replaceWhere", f"business_date = '{s.business_date}'").save(s.rejects))

    if n_bad / max(n_good + n_bad, 1) > s.reject_limit:
        emit("stop", reject_share=round(n_bad / (n_good + n_bad), 3))
        raise RuntimeError("reject share above the limit; target left untouched")

    write_readings(good, s)
    emit("finished", seconds=round(time.time() - t0, 1),
         target_rows=spark.read.format("delta").load(s.target).count())

readings_file = f"{BASE}/meters.json"
with open(readings_file, "w") as fh:
    fh.write('{"meter_id": "M-1", "kwh": "14.2", "status": "ok", "read_at": "2026-10-28 06:00:00"}\n')
    fh.write('{"meter_id": "M-2", "kwh": "n/a", "status": "ok", "read_at": "2026-10-28 06:00:00"}\n')
    fh.write('{"meter_id": "M-3", "kwh": "9.8", "status": "tampered", "read_at": "2026-10-28 06:00:00"}\n')
    fh.write('{"meter_id": "M-4", "kwh": "3.1", "status": "ok"\n')
    for i in range(5, 13):
        fh.write(json.dumps({"meter_id": f"M-{i}", "kwh": f"{i * 1.5:.1f}", "status": "estimated",
                             "read_at": "2026-10-28 06:00:00"}) + "\n")

meter_table = f"file://{BASE}/meter_readings"
spark.createDataFrame([("M-1", 13.9, "ok", "2026-10-27 06:00:00")],
                      "meter_id STRING, kwh DOUBLE, status STRING, read_at STRING") \
     .withColumn("read_at", F.to_timestamp("read_at")).write.format("delta").save(meter_table)

s = Settings(source=f"file://{readings_file}", target=meter_table,
             rejects=f"file://{BASE}/meter_rejects", business_date="2026-10-28")
run(s)
try:
    run(Settings(**{**s.__dict__, "reject_limit": 0.1}))      # a feed that is normally clean
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("strict run:", e)
spark.read.format("delta").load(s.rejects).select("why", "raw", "_bad_line").orderBy("why").show(truncate=60)

spark.stop()

{"business_date": "2026-10-28", "rows": 12, "step": "read"}
{"accepted": 9, "by_reason": {"kwh_not_numeric": 1, "unknown_status": 1, "unparseable_line": 1}, "rejected": 3, "step": "validate"}
{"attempt": 1, "error": "Transient", "fn": "write_readings", "step": "retry"}
{"seconds": 5.4, "step": "finished", "target_rows": 9}
{"business_date": "2026-10-28", "rows": 12, "step": "read"}
{"accepted": 9, "by_reason": {"kwh_not_numeric": 1, "unknown_status": 1, "unparseable_line": 1}, "rejected": 3, "step": "validate"}
{"reject_share": 0.25, "step": "stop"}
strict run: reject share above the limit; target left untouched
+----------------+------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+
|             why|                                                         raw|                                       _bad_line|
+----------------+------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+
| kwh_not_numeric|{"meter_id":"M-2","kwh":"n/a","status":"ok","read_at":"20...|                                            NULL|
|  unknown_status|{"meter_id":"M-3","kwh":"9.8","status":"tampered","read_a...|                                            NULL|
|unparseable_line|                                                          {}|{"meter_id": "M-4", "kwh": "3.1", "status": "ok"|
+----------------+------------------------------------------------------------+------------------------------------------------+

Walk the interviewer through it in this order:

  • Settings in a frozen dataclass. Nothing is hard-coded in the logic, and the business date is passed in, so a backfill is the same call with an older date.
  • One JSON log line per step, with counts. Last night’s rejects become a log query.
  • Rejected rows go to a table, with the reason and the raw input (the truncated line survives intact in _bad_line). It is overwritten per business date, so a rerun replaces rather than duplicates it, and rows can be replayed after a fix.
  • A limit on the reject share. Three bad rows out of twelve (25%) is tolerated at a 30% limit; at 10% the run stops before touching the target, because a sudden jump usually means the source changed.
  • Retry only what can succeed on retry. The storage timeout on the first write was retried with backoff and succeeded; a bad row is never retried.
  • A write that tolerates repetition. The upsert updated M-1 with its newer reading and added eight meters: 9 rows, however many times the job runs.

Streaming and Kafka

139. Kafka partitions, consumer groups and ordering: how many consumers can read a topic in parallel, and what is ordered?
  • A topic is split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, append-only log; each message gets an increasing offset within its partition.
  • Ordering is per partition only. Messages with the same key go to the same partition (the default partitioner hashes the key), so per-key order holds and global order does not.
  • A consumer group shares a topic’s partitions: each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group. Parallelism is capped by the partition count, so 12 partitions and 20 consumers leave 8 idle.
  • Adding or removing a consumer triggers a rebalance, which reassigns partitions.
kafka-topics --bootstrap-server kafka:29092 --create --topic payments \
  --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 --config min.insync.replicas=2

kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server kafka:29092 --describe --group fraud-scorer
# shows CURRENT-OFFSET, LOG-END-OFFSET and LAG for each partition

Durability: with acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2, a write succeeds only when two replicas have it, so losing one broker loses no acknowledged data. Choosing the key is the design decision: key payments by account_id for per-account order, and watch for a hot key that overloads one partition (question 30’s skew, one layer earlier).

Question 38’s run showed the hashing: with 3 partitions and keys A1, A2, A3, the final offsets were {'0': 4, '1': 2, '2': 0}. Partition 2 received nothing, because three keys do not spread evenly over three partitions.

140. Join two streams (ad impressions and clicks). What stops the join state from growing forever?

A stream-stream join keeps both sides in state, waiting for a match. Bound it with a watermark on each side and a time-range condition in the join:

imps = (spark.readStream.schema("ad_id STRING, imp_ts TIMESTAMP").json(f"{src}/impressions")
        .withWatermark("imp_ts", "2 hours"))
clks = (spark.readStream.schema("click_ad_id STRING, click_ts TIMESTAMP").json(f"{src}/clicks")
        .withWatermark("click_ts", "3 hours"))

joined = imps.join(clks, F.expr("""
    click_ad_id = ad_id AND
    click_ts >= imp_ts AND click_ts <= imp_ts + interval 1 hour"""))

q = (joined.writeStream.format("memory").queryName("ad_clicks")
     .option("checkpointLocation", chk).trigger(availableNow=True).start())

Three impressions at 10:00, 10:01 and 10:02; a click on a1 five minutes later, and a click on a2 89 minutes later:

+-----+-------------------+-------------------+
|ad_id|             imp_ts|           click_ts|
+-----+-------------------+-------------------+
|   a1|2026-10-01 10:00:00|2026-10-01 10:05:00|
+-----+-------------------+-------------------+

Only a1 matched: the a2 click is outside the one-hour range. The range condition plus the watermarks tell Spark when an impression can no longer match, so it can drop it from state. Without them the query still runs, but the state of an inner join grows forever. For outer joins, the watermark and range condition are mandatory, because Spark must know when to emit the unmatched row with nulls.

Data modeling

These build on questions 51 to 55. The data modeling guide covers each topic in depth with runnable examples.

141. Model a sales fact for five sales channels and three product hierarchies. What is the grain?

Declare the grain first: one row per order line, the lowest level the sources record. Channel becomes a dimension, not five separate fact tables, so cross-channel totals are a plain GROUP BY:

CREATE TABLE dim_channel (
  channel_sk   INT,
  channel_code STRING,           -- web, app, store, marketplace, wholesale
  channel_type STRING            -- direct / partner
);

CREATE TABLE fact_order_line (
  order_id        STRING,        -- degenerate dimension
  line_number     INT,
  order_date_key  INT,
  channel_sk      INT,
  product_sk      BIGINT,        -- hierarchies live on dim_product
  customer_sk     BIGINT,
  quantity        INT,
  net_amount      DECIMAL(12, 2)
);

SELECT c.channel_code, p.category, SUM(f.net_amount)
FROM fact_order_line f
JOIN dim_channel c ON c.channel_sk = f.channel_sk
JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_sk = f.product_sk
GROUP BY c.channel_code, p.category;

The three product hierarchies (category, brand, merchandising group) are attributes of dim_product, or separate hierarchy tables if they are ragged or change on their own schedule. A hierarchy describes the product, not the sale, so the fact holds only product_sk.

If one channel reports at a coarser level (wholesale sends daily totals, not lines), do not mix it into the line fact. Build a second fact at the daily grain and conform the shared dimensions so the two can be compared.

142. Role-playing, junk and degenerate dimensions.

Role-playing: one physical dimension used in several roles, exposed as views named for the role:

CREATE VIEW dim_order_date    AS SELECT date_key AS order_date_key,    full_date AS order_date    FROM dim_date;
CREATE VIEW dim_ship_date     AS SELECT date_key AS ship_date_key,     full_date AS ship_date     FROM dim_date;
CREATE VIEW dim_delivery_date AS SELECT date_key AS delivery_date_key, full_date AS delivery_date FROM dim_date;

Junk dimension: low-cardinality flags combined into one small dimension, one row per combination, so the fact holds one key instead of many flag columns:

CREATE TABLE dim_order_flags AS
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY is_gift, payment_type, has_promo) AS order_flags_sk,
       is_gift, payment_type, has_promo
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT is_gift, payment_type, has_promo FROM staging.orders) t;

Degenerate dimension: a key with no dimension table, such as order_id on the fact. It groups lines into an order and traces back to the source, and has no attributes of its own to store.

143. What are conformed dimensions, and what is a bus matrix?

A conformed dimension has the same keys, attribute names and meanings in every fact that uses it. Then “drilling across” two facts is valid:

-- Sales and support tickets by the same customer segment
WITH s AS (SELECT c.segment, SUM(f.net_amount) AS revenue
           FROM fact_order_line f JOIN dim_customer c USING (customer_sk) GROUP BY c.segment),
     t AS (SELECT c.segment, COUNT(*) AS tickets
           FROM fact_support_ticket f JOIN dim_customer c USING (customer_sk) GROUP BY c.segment)
SELECT s.segment, s.revenue, t.tickets, t.tickets / (s.revenue / 1000) AS tickets_per_1k_revenue
FROM s JOIN t USING (segment);

Aggregate each fact separately, then join the results on the conformed attribute. Joining the two facts directly would fan out (question 82).

The bus matrix is the planning grid: business processes as rows, dimensions as columns, and a mark where a process uses a dimension:

                   date  customer  product  store  channel
 orders             X       X        X        X       X
 shipments          X       X        X        X
 returns            X       X        X        X       X
 support tickets    X       X        X

It shows which dimensions must be conformed before teams build facts on their own. Without it, each team builds its own customer dimension and the numbers stop agreeing.

144. SCD Type 1 vs Type 2 vs Type 6: how do you choose?

Ask how the business reports history, per attribute:

  • Type 1 when only the current value matters, or the change is a correction. History is restated.
  • Type 2 when facts must report under the value valid at the time: sales by the region the customer was in when they bought.
  • Type 6 when users need both “as was” and “as is” on the same row: Type 2 rows, plus a current_ column overwritten on every version.
-- Type 6: after Ranga moves Pune -> Mumbai, both versions carry the current city
customer_sk | customer_id | city   | current_city | valid_from | valid_to   | is_current
101         | C01         | Pune   | Mumbai       | 2026-01-01 | 2026-03-01 | false
102         | C01         | Mumbai | Mumbai       | 2026-03-01 | NULL       | true

-- "as was": revenue by the city at purchase time
SELECT d.city, SUM(f.net_amount) FROM fact_order_line f JOIN dim_customer d USING (customer_sk) GROUP BY d.city;
-- "as is": the same facts by today's city, with no extra join
SELECT d.current_city, SUM(f.net_amount) FROM fact_order_line f JOIN dim_customer d USING (customer_sk) GROUP BY d.current_city;

The choice is per attribute, not per table: email can be Type 1 while loyalty_tier is Type 2 in the same dimension. Question 51 has the Type 2 MERGE.

145. A fact arrives before its dimension row (an early-arriving fact). What do you load?

Never drop the fact and never load a NULL key. The standard answer is an inferred member: insert a placeholder dimension row with the business key, then overwrite it in place when the real row arrives:

-- 1. Before loading facts: create placeholders for unknown business keys
INSERT INTO dim_customer (customer_sk, customer_id, city, is_inferred, valid_from, is_current)
SELECT next_sk(), s.customer_id, 'Unknown', true, s.order_date, true
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS order_date
      FROM staging.orders GROUP BY customer_id) s
LEFT ANTI JOIN dim_customer d ON d.customer_id = s.customer_id;

-- 2. When the real customer row arrives: a Type 1 overwrite of the placeholder,
--    even in a Type 2 dimension, so the facts' keys stay valid
MERGE INTO dim_customer t
USING staging.customers s
ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id AND t.is_inferred
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET city = s.city, is_inferred = false;

(next_sk() stands for your surrogate-key generator, such as an identity column.) The alternative is pointing the fact at a reserved unknown member (-1) and reprocessing the fact later. The inferred member avoids that reprocessing. Monitor how many inferred rows are never completed.

146. One big table (OBT) vs a star schema in a lakehouse.

An OBT pre-joins the fact with its dimension attributes:

CREATE TABLE gold.sales_obt USING delta AS
SELECT f.order_id, f.order_date_key, f.quantity, f.net_amount,
       c.segment, c.city, p.category, p.brand, ch.channel_code
FROM fact_order_line f
JOIN dim_customer c ON c.customer_sk = f.customer_sk
JOIN dim_product  p ON p.product_sk  = f.product_sk
JOIN dim_channel ch ON ch.channel_sk = f.channel_sk;

Columnar formats read only the columns a query needs and compress repeated values well, so wide tables are much cheaper than they were in a row store, and dashboards get join-free SQL.

What an OBT costs: a Type 1 dimension change means rewriting every fact row that carries the attribute; the history semantics are frozen when the table is built; and every new attribute is a backfill.

A defensible answer keeps the star as the source of truth and derives OBTs for specific dashboards, rebuilt from the star whenever needed.

System design

Expect one system design round at most product companies. The 2026 guides describe it as the round that carries the most weight. The follow-ups are predictable: why this storage layer, what you ruled out, how backfill works, what breaks when a source changes, and what it costs over time.

147. Design a pipeline that ingests 1 TB of clickstream a day and serves dashboards at under 2 seconds P95.

Start with the numbers: 1 TB a day is about 12 MB/s on average, so plan for 3 to 5 times that at peak. Then the layers:

 SDK / web ──► Kafka (partition by user_id) ──► stream job ──► bronze table
                                                     │          (append, raw)
                                                     ▼
                                    silver: deduplicated, sessionized events
                                                     │
                                                     ▼
              gold: pre-aggregated by minute/hour × dimension ──► serving store
                                                                  (OLAP engine)

The key decision is that dashboards never scan raw events. Two seconds at P95 comes from pre-aggregated gold tables, or from a real-time OLAP store (Druid, Pinot, ClickHouse), not from a lake query over a terabyte. The gold step is a windowed aggregate:

events = (spark.readStream.table("bronze.clicks")
          .withWatermark("event_ts", "15 minutes")
          .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]))

per_minute = (events
    .groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "1 minute"), "page", "country")
    .agg(F.count("*").alias("views"), F.approx_count_distinct("user_id").alias("users")))

(per_minute.writeStream.outputMode("append")
   .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://lake/_chk/clicks_per_minute")
   .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")
   .toTable("gold.clicks_per_minute"))

Cover deduplication by event ID, late events with a watermark, a schema registry for the event contract, partitioning by event date, and compaction of the small files that streaming writes (question 36).

The follow-ups: the Kafka partition count comes from peak throughput per partition and consumer parallelism; and a day is replayed from bronze, not from Kafka, once Kafka’s retention has passed.

148. Backfill nine months of history after a logic fix, without double counting and without stopping the daily job.

Make every run partition-scoped and overwrite-based, so a backfill is just the normal job run with old dates:

from datetime import date, timedelta
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def run_day(d):
    df = transform(spark.read.table("silver.orders").filter(F.col("order_date") == d))
    (df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite")
       .option("replaceWhere", f"order_date = '{d}'")       # replaces exactly one day
       .saveAsTable("gold_shadow.daily_sales"))             # a copy, not the live table
    return d

days = [date(2026, 1, 1) + timedelta(n) for n in range(273)]
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:              # throttle: the daily job still runs
    for d in pool.map(run_day, reversed(days)):              # newest months first
        print("done", d)
  • Write to a shadow table first, reconcile its counts and totals against the live table, then swap.
  • Throttle with a small worker pool so the backfill does not starve the daily SLA.
  • Freeze the inputs: read a fixed snapshot of silver (VERSION AS OF), not a table that is still changing.

The trap: appending recomputed data on top of the old output. That is the double count. Overwrite-by-partition makes reruns safe, including a rerun of the backfill itself.

149. An upstream API changes a field from a string to an object, and the pipeline starts failing. What do you do in the next hour?

In order:

  1. Stop the damage. Pause the job, or let it fail closed. Do not let it write partial or mis-parsed data into tables consumers read.
  2. Keep the raw data. Make sure bronze still lands raw payloads, so nothing is lost while you fix the parser.
  3. Tell people: which tables are stale, since when, and when you will update them next.
  4. Fix forward: parse both shapes, and route anything unparseable to quarantine.
  5. Replay from bronze for the affected window, then reconcile the counts.

Step 4 in PySpark, when customer changed from "C01" to {"id": "C01", "tier": "gold"}:

raw = spark.read.table("bronze.orders_raw")                  # payload kept as a string

parsed = raw.select(
    F.get_json_object("payload", "$.order_id").alias("order_id"),
    F.coalesce(
        F.get_json_object("payload", "$.customer.id"),       # new shape: object
        F.when(~F.get_json_object("payload", "$.customer").startswith("{"),
               F.get_json_object("payload", "$.customer"))   # old shape: plain string
    ).alias("customer_id"),
    "payload")

parsed.filter("customer_id IS NULL").write.mode("append").saveAsTable("quarantine.orders")
parsed.filter("customer_id IS NOT NULL").drop("payload").createOrReplaceTempView("fixed")

One payload of each shape, plus one with no customer:

+--------+-----------+
|order_id|customer_id|
+--------+-----------+
|      o1|        C01|
|      o2|        C02|
|      o3|       NULL|
+--------+-----------+

Afterwards: a schema contract with the producer, a schema check at ingestion that alerts before the transform fails, and a test with the new payload.

150. Design CDC replication from a PostgreSQL OLTP database into a lakehouse table. 
 PostgreSQL WAL ──► Debezium (logical replication slot) ──► Kafka topic per table
                                                                 │
          initial snapshot ─────────────────────────────────────┤
                                                                 ▼
                         Spark: latest change per key by LSN, then MERGE

The Debezium connector, registered with Kafka Connect:

{
  "name": "orders-cdc",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "plugin.name": "pgoutput",
    "database.hostname": "orders-db", "database.port": "5432",
    "database.user": "debezium", "database.password": "${file:/secrets/db.properties:password}",
    "database.dbname": "shop",
    "topic.prefix": "shop",
    "table.include.list": "public.orders",
    "slot.name": "orders_cdc",
    "snapshot.mode": "initial"
  }
}

The apply step keeps the newest change per key and ignores anything older than what the target already has:

w = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.desc("lsn"))
latest = (changes.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rn = 1").drop("rn"))

(DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.orders").alias("t")
   .merge(latest.alias("s"), "t.order_id = s.order_id")
   .whenMatchedDelete(condition="s.op = 'd' AND s.lsn > t.lsn")
   .whenMatchedUpdate(condition="s.op <> 'd' AND s.lsn > t.lsn",
                      set={"status": "s.status", "lsn": "s.lsn"})
   .whenNotMatchedInsert(condition="s.op <> 'd'",
                         values={"order_id": "s.order_id", "status": "s.status", "lsn": "s.lsn"})
   .execute())

The target starts with orders 1 and 2 at LSN 100. Five changes arrive out of order: two updates to order 1 (LSN 103 and 105), a delete of order 2 at 104, a stale update of order 2 at 99, and a new order 3:

+--------+-------+---+
|order_id| status|lsn|
+--------+-------+---+
|       1|shipped|105|
|       3| placed|106|
+--------+-------+---+

Order 1 took the LSN 105 update, not 103. Order 2 was deleted, because the newest change for it (104) is the delete, and the stale LSN 99 update lost the ROW_NUMBER. Order 3 was inserted.

The operational risk to name: a replication slot that nobody consumes keeps WAL on the primary until its disk fills. Monitor slot lag:

SELECT slot_name, active,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), confirmed_flush_lsn)) AS retained_wal
FROM pg_replication_slots;

The data modeling guide runs an idempotent CDC apply end to end, including what a late event does after a hard delete.

151. Estimate storage and cost at one, three and ten years for a 500 GB-a-day source.

Interviewers want arithmetic, stated assumptions and the levers that change the result:

raw_gb_per_day = 500
compression = 5          # assumption: measure it on a sample
layers = 2.2             # bronze + silver + a smaller gold
retained_versions = 1.1  # time travel keeps some old files alive
usd_per_gb_month = 0.023 # object storage, standard class

for years in (1, 3, 10):
    tb = raw_gb_per_day * 365 * years / compression * layers * retained_versions / 1024
    print(f"{years:>2} years: {tb:6.0f} TB stored, about ${tb * 1024 * usd_per_gb_month:,.0f} a month")

 1 years:     86 TB stored, about $2,032 a month
 3 years:    259 TB stored, about $6,095 a month
10 years:    863 TB stored, about $20,316 a month

Then the levers: lifecycle rules that move old bronze to colder storage classes (question 75), a retention policy per layer, snapshot expiry and orphan-file cleanup, and aggregating old detail nobody queries. Compute usually costs more than storage, so mention incremental processing, which avoids recomputing history every day.

152. Design an event deduplication layer for at-least-once delivery at billions of events a day.

At-least-once delivery makes duplicates normal, so deduplication is a design component, not a cleanup job. Two layers:

deduped = (spark.readStream.table("bronze.events")
           .withWatermark("event_ts", "2 hours")              # longest realistic redelivery
           .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]))      # layer 1: bounded state

def upsert(batch_df, batch_id):                                # layer 2: idempotent sink
    (DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.events").alias("t")
       .merge(batch_df.alias("s"), "t.event_date = s.event_date AND t.event_id = s.event_id")
       .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
       .execute())

deduped.writeStream.foreachBatch(upsert).option("checkpointLocation", chk).start()
  • Key: a producer-assigned event ID. Without one, hash the business fields, and accept that two identical genuine events will merge.
  • Window: state with a watermark, sized to the longest redelivery delay. Question 38 showed it catching a producer retry inside one batch and resent events across runs.
  • Sink: the MERGE catches duplicates that arrive after the state has expired.
  • Measure: track the duplicate rate. A sudden rise usually means a producer retry storm, not more traffic.

Airflow

These DAGs were loaded with DagBag and the fan-out DAG was test-run with airflow dags test on Airflow 3.1.0.

153. How do you make an Airflow DAG idempotent?

Each task run must process a fixed slice of data and produce the same output however many times it runs. Question 74’s DAG shows all three rules:

  • Use the data interval, not the clock. The task takes data_interval_start and data_interval_end from the run context instead of calling datetime.now(). Rerunning last Tuesday then processes last Tuesday.
  • Overwrite the slice the task owns (INSERT OVERWRITE ... PARTITION), or MERGE on a key. Never append.
  • Keep tasks atomic. Write to staging and swap, so a failed attempt leaves nothing for the retry to trip over.
@task
def load_partition(data_interval_start=None, data_interval_end=None):
    # Airflow fills these from the run being executed
    run_sql(f"""
        INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE sales.orders PARTITION (order_date = '{data_interval_start:%Y-%m-%d}')
        SELECT * FROM staging.orders
        WHERE event_ts >= '{data_interval_start}' AND event_ts < '{data_interval_end}'
    """)

The trap: a task that “loads everything since the last run” using a watermark stored outside Airflow. A manual rerun of an old interval then loads whatever is new today, not that interval’s data.

154. catchup, backfill, and what happens when you deploy a DAG with a start_date in the past.

With catchup=True, the scheduler creates a run for every interval between start_date and now that has not run. Deploying a daily DAG with a start_date a year ago creates 365 runs at once. With catchup=False, only the latest interval runs.

Set it on every DAG. The default comes from catchup_by_default, which Airflow 3 changed from True to False, so the same DAG file behaves differently after an upgrade. The loaded DAGs confirm the setting:

from airflow.models.dagbag import DagBag

bag = DagBag("/opt/airflow/dags", include_examples=False)
print("import errors:", bag.import_errors)
for dag_id, dag in sorted(bag.dags.items()):
    print(dag_id, "catchup=", dag.catchup, "tasks=", [t.task_id for t in dag.tasks])

import errors: {}
daily_orders catchup= False tasks= ['wait_for_file', 'load_partition']
file_fanout catchup= False tasks= ['list_files', 'process', 'publish']
orders_report catchup= False tasks= ['build_report']

Run deliberate backfills with the CLI, throttled:

airflow backfill create --dag-id daily_orders \
  --from-date 2026-01-01 --to-date 2026-09-30 --max-active-runs 3
